p132: 132.  Furthermore, the possibility for a State to grant an amnesty to the perpetrators of grave breaches of human rights may be circumscribed by treaties to which the State is a party. A number of international conventions provide for a duty to prosecute the perpetrators of certain crimes defined therein (see the 1949 Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of war and their Additional Protocols, in particular Article 3 common to those Conventions; Articles 49 and 50 of the Convention (I) for the Amelioration of the Condition of the Wounded and Sick in Armed Forces in the Field; Articles 50 and 51 of the Convention (II) for the Amelioration of the Condition of Wounded, Sick and Shipwrecked Members of Armed Forces at Sea; Articles 129 and 130 of the Convention (III) relative to the Treatment of Prisoners of War; and Articles 146 and 147 of the Convention (IV) relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War; see also Articles 4 and 13 of the 1977 Additional Protocol (II) to the Geneva Conventions relating to the Protection of Victims of Non-International Armed Conflicts, Article V of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, and the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment).
p133: 133.  The Convention on the Non-Applicability of Statutory Limitations to War Crimes and Crimes against Humanity prohibits statutory limitations in respect of both those categories of crimes.
p134: 134.  Various international bodies have issued resolutions, recommendations or comments concerning impunity and the granting of amnesties in respect of grave breaches of human rights, generally indicating that the perpetrators of such violations of human rights and international humanitarian law should not be granted amnesty (see paragraphs 45, 47-49, 51-53 and 56-58 above).
p135: 135.  Several international courts have held that amnesties cannot be accepted where they are intended to prevent the investigation of grave breaches of human rights or of acts constituting crimes under international law and the punishment of those responsible for such abuses (see paragraphs 54 and 59-68 above).
p136: 136.  Although the wording of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 confines its application to the national level, it should be noted that the scope of certain international instruments extends to a retrial in another State or before an international tribunal. For example, Article 20 of the ICC Statute contains an explicit exception to the ne bis in idem principle, as it allows the ICC to try a person already acquitted by another court of genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes if the proceedings in the other court were for the purpose of shielding the person concerned from criminal responsibility for crimes within the jurisdiction of the ICC.
p137: 137.  The Court takes note of the third-party intervener’s argument that there is a lack of consensus among States at the international level as to an absolute prohibition of the use of amnesty for grave breaches of fundamental human rights, in particular those guaranteed by Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The third-party intervener also expressed the view that amnesty, when used as a means of bringing prolonged conflicts to an end, may lead to positive outcomes (see the third-party intervener’s submissions summarised in paragraphs 108-113 above).
p138: 138.  The Court also takes note of the case-law of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, notably the cases of Barrios Altos, Gomes Lund et al., Gelman and Massacres of El Mozote and nearby places, all cited above, in which that court, relying on its previous case-law and on the findings of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, the United Nations bodies and other universal and regional human rights protection bodies, took a firm stance on the issue, holding that no amnesty could be accepted in respect of grave breaches of fundamental human rights. It explained that in such cases an amnesty would seriously undermine the States’ obligation to investigate such abuses and to punish their perpetrators (see Gelman, cited above, § 195, and Gomes Lund et al., cited above, § 171). The Inter-American Court emphasised that such amnesties contravened non-derogable rights recognised by international human rights law (see Gomes Lund et al., § 171).
